title: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems

object.carrier: Permissioned blockchain ledger holding DID documents, issuer identifiers, credential schemas, revocation registries and trust scores; verifiable credentials held off-chain by their agents; long-term ML-KEM public keys pre-distributed into and cached in DID documents. Lifecycle is explicitly discussed: issuance (VCs signed by a trusted issuer under JIT, task-scoped), update (key rotation triggered by monitoring, DID-document update transactions, periodic on-chain snapshots), retention (immutable, logged DID history), retrieval (agents discover each other's DIDs/permissions via the ledger; verifiers check credential status), revocation (smart-contract deactivation of DIDs and global credential revocation; VCs below the trust floor auto-revoked). DIDs/ledger are long-lived; JIT VCs are scoped to a single task runtime, hence scope=mixed.

safety_property.statement: Targets confidentiality + integrity of inter-agent messages together with least-privilege authority over agent identities. Mutually authenticated, crypto-agile mTLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment (AEAD payloads, e.g., AES-256-GCM) protects messages in transit against eavesdropping and MiTM; DID + task-scoped JIT verifiable credentials with on-chain revocation bound to least privilege restrict what an agent (possibly compromised) may do; signed CBOR/COSE envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges; optional ZKPs verify that a delegated payload conforms to the committed task policy without disclosure. Stated failure conditions: a ZKP still validates hallucinated/malicious results that conform to policy (no semantic-correctness attestation); a revoked agent may connect during the block-time finality window; PQC implementations are immature. No property is empirically evaluated - the paper is a theoretical architecture.
safety_property.operationalized_as: None - no experiments, simulations or benchmarks. The property is argued via threat analysis (§3) and architectural specification (§4); the authors themselves call for empirical tests (COSE overhead, hybrid mTLS latency, KEMTLS-PDK gains, scalability) in §7-§8.

capabilities: Impersonate agents and manipulate the orchestrator via typo-squatting and synonymously named agents/resources (shadowing attacks), engaging malicious agents or tools
Intercept, inject and modify inter-agent messages (MiTM); passively eavesdrop, including harvest-now-decrypt-later until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer breaks RSA/ECC
Direct and indirect prompt injection into documents/prompts the agent parses, leading to RAG and memory poisoning, data leaks, flooding attacks and resource waste
Rug pull: first supply a benign, approved agent/tool, then exhibit anomalous malicious behavior after updates, abusing acquired trust and permission levels
Compromise an agent and abuse its permissions; as a malicious intermediary, tamper with the Protobuf payload before forwarding to the next hop
Attack orchestration/reasoning to drive denial-of-wallet, cascading failures and privilege escalation (a user-facing agent delegating an unsafe action to a more privileged agent)
Quantum adversary substituting an agent's KEM key if ledger transactions registering DID documents are not themselves PQC-signed
Malicious developers / compromised MCP servers distributed through marketplaces
assumptions: Agents communicate over local or public networks, with sensitive information exchanged across differing trust levels; which measures apply is deployment-context dependent
A permissioned ledger is available as the root of trust for KEM keys; transactions registering and updating DID documents must themselves be secured by PQC signatures
Symmetric AEAD with 256-bit keys remains secure against HNDL; post-quantum schemes (ML-KEM, ML-DSA/FN-DSA, hybrid X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3) hold
Trusted issuers attest agent attributes; SPIFFE/SVID-style infrastructure binds agent key pairs to identities (SVIDs ephemeral)
Runtime monitoring supplies telemetry so a trust-evaluation service can score agents and smart contracts can rotate keys or revoke VCs
not_covered: Semantic correctness of model outputs: hallucinated or malicious results still yield a valid ZKP as long as they conform to policy
Threats originating from the MCP servers themselves ('It will not address all of the challenges faced by MCP as some of them originate from the MCP servers themselves.')
Malicious-developer attacks despite marketplace cryptographic validation ('this solution is not enough')
The brief vulnerability window before ledger finality, during which a revoked agent may still establish connections
Implementation-level side channels and cryptanalytic breaks in young PQC (side-channel vulnerabilities in early ML-KEM implementations; SIKE and Rainbow breaks)
No empirical evaluation of any proposed mechanism

intervention.name: Zero-trust cryptographic agent-to-agent communication architecture: DID/VC identity on a permissioned ledger + KEMTLS-PDK hybrid post-quantum mTLS + signed CBOR/COSE envelopes + ZKP intent verification + trust-threshold monitoring
intervention.description: A synthesized architecture (survey/position paper, not a built system): agent identities as DIDs with task-scoped JIT verifiable credentials anchored on a permissioned ledger with on-chain revocation; mutually authenticated crypto-agile mTLS with hybrid PQ/T key exchange, upgraded to KEMTLS-PDK by pre-distributing long-term ML-KEM public keys in DID documents to cut handshake overhead; immutable CBOR/COSE message envelopes for multi-hop payload integrity; optional zk-SNARK/zk-STARK proofs that delegated payloads satisfy the task-policy commitment; a trust-threshold layer scores observed behavior and gates task assignment, with smart-contract revocation below the global minimum.

results.claim: Post-quantum signatures are far larger than classical ones - ML-DSA signatures span 2420-4627 bytes depending on security level vs 64 bytes for ECDSA - which can bloat certificate chains, exceed the initial TCP congestion window and add round trips/fragmentation, motivating hybrid key exchange, more compact signatures, certificate compression and KEMTLS-PDK.
results.setting: Cryptographic size comparison stated in §4.2 (sizes from the PQC literature, no experiment by the authors); concerns TLS handshake/certificate-chain transmission in agent-to-agent communication, particularly on constrained links such as drones and IoT devices.
results.quote: Comparing ML-DSA signature, which is 2420 to 4627 bytes long depending on the security level, to 64 bytes long signatures for ECDSA, we can observe a huge difference in weight.

results.claim: KEMTLS-PDK authenticates the responder within the first round trip and eliminates certificate transmission; the paper proposes that MAS use it by pre-distributing long-term ML-KEM public keys into agents' DID documents during discovery, so the initiator encapsulates the shared secret to the responder's cached public key, offsetting post-quantum cost.
results.value: single flight: responder authenticated in first round trip; certificate transmission eliminated
results.comparison: vs KEMTLS with online handshake using heavy PQC signatures, where post-quantum signatures remain in the certificate chain
results.setting: Proposed transport design (§4.2, Figure 2): zero-trust MAS where agents discover each other's DIDs/permissions through a ledger-based registry; design adopted from the KEMTLS-PDK literature, no simulation run - the paper explicitly asks for empirical measurement of the latency reduction.
results.quote: A secret to this key can be encapsulated in its first sent message, which authenticates the responder within the first round trip and eliminates the transmission of the certificate.

results.claim: For succinct proof systems (e.g., zk-SNARKs), proof verification is claimed to take milliseconds regardless of the size of the underlying computation, while proof generation remains computationally expensive - the asymmetry the ZKP intent-verification mechanism relies on.
results.setting: General claim about succinct proof systems within the proposed architecture: the receiving agent verifies the delegated payload against the policy commitment embedded in the JIT VC; no benchmark performed by the authors.
results.quote: for succinct proof systems, verification takes milliseconds regardless of the size of the underlying computation, whereas proof generation remains computationally expensive.

results.claim: Design premise of the transport layer: symmetric AEAD ciphers with 256-bit keys (e.g., AES-256-GCM) remain secure against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks, while asymmetric RSA/ECC does not survive a cryptographically relevant quantum computer - hence post-quantum / hybrid mTLS is treated as obligatory for agent-to-agent traffic.
results.value: symmetric AEAD with 256-bit keys secure; asymmetric (RSA/ECC) not
results.setting: Stated cryptographic premise underpinning the post-quantum transport proposal for inter-agent messages that can carry valuable business information; not experimentally established in the paper.
results.quote: While symmetric AEAD ciphers with 256-bit keys remain secure against harvest now decrypt later attacks (HNDL), asymmetric cryptography does not.

limitations.statement: Primary bottleneck is the computational intensity of ZKP generation: compiling an agent's execution trace into an arithmetic circuit and generating the zk-SNARK could induce unacceptable delays when coupled with high LLM-inference latency.
limitations.quote: The primary bottleneck lies in the computational intensity of generating ZKPs.

limitations.statement: Envelope accumulation: as each agent appends its own proof, the COSE payload grows linearly with execution-chain depth and can strain edge-node memory; recursive ZKPs are proposed as future work to keep envelope size constant.
limitations.quote: As each agent appends its own proof leading to a linear growth in payload size it can eventually strain the memory limits of edge nodes.

limitations.statement: Blockchain-registry revocation leaves a brief vulnerability window tied to block-time finality, during which a revoked but previously authenticated agent might still establish a new connection.
limitations.quote: Furthermore, the reliance on a blockchain registry to enforce dynamic least privilege introduces a brief vulnerability window tied to block-time finality, during which a revoked but previously authenticated agent might attempt to establish a new connection before the network consensus fully registers its revocation.

limitations.statement: The study is primarily theoretical: no empirical tests or benchmarks exist (overhead of CBOR/COSE message-level protection, hybrid mTLS latency, whether KEMTLS-PDK resolves it, ZKP validity, scalability, dynamic environments).
limitations.quote: Because this study is primarily theoretical, these topics require additional empirical tests and benchmarks, e.g., measuring the overhead of message-level protection with CBOR and COSE.

limitations.statement: ZKPs limit rather than prevent malicious or hallucinated outcomes: any result conforming to the committed policy yields a valid proof, and the proof does not attest the semantic correctness of the model's output.
limitations.quote: Hallucinated or malicious results caused by threat actors will still yield a valid proof as long as it conforms to the policy.

limitations.statement: PQC algorithms/implementations are young and under-cryptanalyzed (SIKE and Rainbow breaks, side channels in early ML-KEM), so exclusive reliance is premature - hybrid PQ/T first; additionally, current zk-SNARKs rely on non-quantum-resistant elliptic-curve pairings (zk-STARKs suggested instead).
limitations.quote: For now, they are too immature to just start exclusively relying on them.
